hook.line: Every weekend starts with the same question. Today you can answer it, and ask it back.
hook.es:
¿Qué vas a hacer el sábado?
Voy a bailar con Vale.
hook.en:
What are you going to do on Saturday?
I'm going to dance with Vale.

examples.en: I'm going to cook on Sunday.
Are you going to watch the match?

examples.es: Mariana va a escribir sobre la fiesta.
examples.en: Mariana is going to write about the party.

examples.es: Vamos a caminar en el parque.
examples.en: We're going to walk in the park.

examples.es: Los clientes van a pasar el día en el café.
examples.en: The customers are going to spend the day at the café.

rule:
To talk about plans, use *ir* (to go) + *a* + the plain verb. It's exactly 'going to' in English.

*voy a*, *vas a*, *va a*, *vamos a*, *van a* + *cocinar*, *bailar*, *hacer…*

*Voy a cocinar el domingo. ¿Vas a ver el partido? Vamos a caminar.*

The second verb never changes: it's always the form ending in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*.

To say no, put *no* before the *ir* part: *No voy a cantar.*

To ask someone their plans: *¿Qué vas a hacer el sábado?*

In Latin America this is the everyday way to talk about the future. You'll hear it far more than any other future form.

And *vamos a* + verb on its own, with the right tone, is also 'let's': *¡Vamos a bailar!*
smallPrint: This is the periphrastic future: *ir a* + infinitive.
soundTip: In fast speech *voy a* sounds like one word, '*voya*', and *vamos a* like '*vamosa*'.

options: I swim on Saturdays.
I'm going to swim on Saturday.
I'm going to the pool on Saturday.
Are you going to cook?
Do you cook?
Is she going to cook?
They're going to watch a film.
I'm going to watch a film.

readAndPick.es: Vale y Tomás van a pasar el domingo en el centro.
options: Vale and Tomás live downtown.
We're going to spend Sunday downtown.
Vale and Tomás are going to spend Sunday downtown.

readAndPick.es: No voy a trabajar el lunes.
options: I'm not going to work on Monday.
I don't work on Mondays.
I'm going to work on Monday.

readAndPick.es: Don Hernando va a dejar el libro aquí.
options: Don Hernando leaves the book here every day.
Don Hernando is going to leave the book here.
I'm going to leave the book here.
What are you all going to do?
What are we going to do?
What is he going to do?

readAndPick.es: Va a ser un año chévere.
options: It was a great year.
It's a great year.
It's going to be a great year.
Simón sings every day.
Simón is going to sing now.
Simón doesn't sing.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I'm going to cook on Sunday.
Ask a friend: what are you going to do on Saturday?
yourTurn.why: *Tú* is *vas*; the second verb stays plain: *hacer*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Mariana is going to watch the match.
yourTurn.answer: Mariana va a ver el partido.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I'm not going to sing.
Ask a group of friends if they're going to walk in the park.
accept: ¿Ustedes van a caminar en el parque?

yourTurn.prompt: Say: It's going to be a great party.
yourTurn.answer: Va a ser una fiesta chévere.
yourTurn.why: *Ir a* works with *ser* too: *va a ser*.

pitfalls.why: The *a* is not optional: *voy a* + verb.
After *voy a* the verb stays plain, ending in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*.
*No* goes in front of the *ir* part.

personal: What are you going to do this weekend? Write two plans with *Voy a…*, and one thing you're not going to do.
